extra.message: User input from content['search'] is directly interpolated into a SQL query string using Python %s formatting, then executed via db.engine.execute(). This allows an attacker to inject arbitrary SQL and extract or modify database contents.

request.url is inserted into an HTML template via Python %s string formatting (line 112), then passed to render_template_string() (line 114). An attacker can inject Jinja2 template syntax (e.g. {{ config }} or {{ dir }}) via the URL path, which will be executed server-side. The template context is further compromised by passing dir=dir, help=help, locals=locals which provide access to Python builtins and the local scope, enabling remote code execution.

request.url is inserted directly into an HTML template via Python %s string formatting without escaping, creating a reflected XSS vulnerability. An attacker can craft a URL containing JavaScript (e.g. <script>alert(1)</script>) which will be rendered in the browser of any user who visits the crafted link.

The exception string str(e) from a failed SQL query is inserted into an HTML template via Python %s formatting (line 280), then passed to render_template_string() (line 281). Since the SQL error message often includes user input, an attacker can inject Jinja2 template syntax via the search parameter, which will be executed server-side. The template context passes dir=dir, help=help, locals=locals enabling remote code execution.

The exception string str(e) is inserted directly into HTML via Python %s string formatting without escaping. Since SQL errors often reflect user input (the search term), this creates a reflected XSS vulnerability where an attacker can inject JavaScript via the search parameter.

The insecure_verify() function decodes JWT tokens with verify=False, completely skipping signature verification. This means any attacker can forge a valid-looking JWT token and it will be accepted. This function is used for authentication in the /get/<cust_id> endpoint (line 227), allowing complete authentication bypass.

The /get/<cust_id> endpoint uses insecure_verify(token) for authentication, which decodes the JWT without verifying the signature (verify=False on line 97). An attacker can craft any JWT token and it will be accepted, allowing unauthenticated access to any customer record.

Three hardcoded secret keys are defined: SECRET_KEY_HMAC='secret' (line 26), SECRET_KEY_HMAC_2='am0r3C0mpl3xK3y' (line 27), and app.secret_key (line 28). These are used for JWT signing and Flask session security. Anyone with access to the source code can forge JWT tokens and session cookies.
Hardcoded admin credentials: username='admin' and password='admin123' are used to seed the database. These are weak, well-known credentials that can be used to authenticate to the application.

yaml.load(y) is called without specifying a SafeLoader. With PyYAML 3.12, this defaults to the unsafe Loader which allows arbitrary Python object deserialization. An attacker can upload a YAML file containing !!python/object/apply: directives to execute arbitrary code on the server.

User passwords are hashed using MD5 (hashlib.md5(password).hexdigest()), which is cryptographically broken and unsuitable for password hashing. MD5 is vulnerable to collision attacks and can be brute-forced rapidly with modern hardware. Should use a dedicated password hashing algorithm like bcrypt or argon2.

The /fetch/customer endpoint returns the customer's credit card number (ccn) in the API response (line 211: 'cc_num': customer_record.ccn). Sensitive financial data should never be returned in full; it should be masked or omitted entirely.

The /get/<cust_id> endpoint returns the customer's credit card number (ccn) in the API response (line 235: 'cc_num': customer_record.ccn). Sensitive financial data should never be returned in full; it should be masked or omitted entirely.

The /fetch/customer endpoint retrieves a customer record by ID (Customer.query.get(customer_id)) without checking that the authenticated user is authorized to access that specific record. Any authenticated user can access any customer's data by changing the ID value, resulting in an Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR).

cwe: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key

extra.message: The /get/<cust_id> endpoint retrieves a customer record by ID from the URL path (Customer.query.get(cust_id)) without any authorization check. Combined with the insecure JWT verification, any unauthenticated attacker can access any customer's data by guessing or iterating IDs.

cwe: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key

extra.message: User-uploaded DOCX files are parsed using Document() from python-docx (which internally uses lxml 4.2.1). This version of lxml is vulnerable to XML External Entity (XXE) attacks by default. An attacker can upload a malicious DOCX file containing XXE payloads to read arbitrary files or perform SSRF.

cwe: CWE-611: Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference

extra.message: The /xxe_uploader endpoint allows unauthenticated users to upload and process files. There is no authentication check (no Authorization header verification) before accepting and processing uploaded files. This allows any anonymous user to exploit the XXE vulnerability.

cwe: CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function

extra.message: The /yaml_hammer endpoint allows unauthenticated users to upload and process YAML files. There is no authentication check before accepting and processing uploaded files. This allows any anonymous user to exploit the insecure YAML deserialization vulnerability for remote code execution.

cwe: CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function

extra.message: The Customer model stores passwords in plaintext (db.Column(db.String(150)) with no hashing applied). When customers are created via /register/customer, the password is stored directly without any hashing (line 161), unlike the User model which at least uses MD5. Plaintext password storage means any database compromise exposes all customer passwords directly.

cwe: CWE-256: Plaintext Storage of a Password
